Ever since the French Concession's Municipal Council had run a road along the north bank of the Zhaojiabang, this old water-route through the southern city had grown narrower and narrower. In winter especially, a long reach of the embankment lay exposed, refuse and silt churned together, and the water was no longer as clean as it once had been. In spring and summer, when the creek ran full, it was often crowded with wooden boats large and small; just now, though, there were only a few, all of them moored along the bank.

Just past four o'clock, cooking smoke began to rise from the bows. Long planks bridged the gap between boat and bank, and on a few of the boats children in their new holiday clothes went racing aboard one moment and leaping ashore the next, wholly heedless of the water and silt beneath the planks.

The Zhaojiabang was crossed by many bridges, and the Maochang Coal Company stood near the little wooden bridge. Since the firm did its trade within the Concession, it naturally had to sit on the creek's north bank; but the Xujiahui Road district had lately grown very prosperous, its waste ground taken over by factories and soy-sauce works, and even a film studio had put up its sound stages nearby. Behind the Maochang there had once been a storage yard, but as the business grew the yard gradually proved too small, and after much deliberation the firm bought a large tract of empty land in the Chinese city on the creek's south bank to serve as its coal yard. Happily, the little wooden bridge joined the two banks of the creek.

Li Han was a worker at the Maochang Coal Company, but he worked in the coal yard, which set him somewhat apart from the men across the water at the firm itself. Over there was a commercial house, dealing day in and day out with the customers who came to buy coal. Here, all one ever saw was coal. For that reason the Maochang's proprietor hired his men for the firm and for the yard by two different rules. For the firm he took on local men, worldly and quick-witted, who could hold a conversation with a customer; for the yard he looked only at whether a man had a pair of strong arms. These past two years the lower Yangtze had flooded, and countrymen, hearing that in Shanghai a man could at least get a mouthful to eat, had found themselves a boat and sculled their way down. The yard was full of such men. Having nowhere to live in Shanghai, they had squatted on the waste ground nearby and thrown up shacks, first of planks, and then, once they had earned a little, contriving to get hold of some cinder-and-mud bricks to make the thing look more like a house. Over the years the yard's people had all come to live clustered together.

On New Year's Eve Li Han had stood watch in the yard the whole night through, never going back to his shack. The New Year was always a time of dread for the yard: the whole city was setting off firecrackers, and if a coal heap were to catch, that would be no small matter. At such times the counting-house always came to Li Han, knowing that among the workers there were several who would listen to no one but him. So the evening before, Li Han had gathered a few men, bought a little wine and meat, and seen the old year out there in the yard.

After daybreak the others had all gone back to their rooms to sleep, but Li Han waited on in the yard. He was waiting for the comrades withdrawing from the Zhonghui Trust Bank on Tianjin Road. Yet it was now past four in the afternoon and still no one had come, and Li Han was growing uneasy.

They had failed to reach the yard at the appointed hour because a great many things had gone unexpectedly wrong. Chen Qianli had to admit that the original plan had carried too much risk. It had all come up so suddenly, in far too much haste. The greatest risk was this: if he had judged wrong, and the enemy, on discovering they had been duped, at once threw a cordon round the scene and made their arrests—would he not then have doomed Comrade Lin Shi?

He had thought it all through, to be sure, and reckoned that since the enemy had let the comrades out of the detention house, they must be waiting for a chance to catch them red-handed, goods and all; and he had, besides, planted a great deal of false information in advance.

The evening before, at the dinner table in the clinic, he had told them all that once the bank operation was done each of them was to return to his present lodging and await the next move. He had also told Cui Wentai that, having got the suitcase, he was to drive the car to the rendezvous at Laozha Bridge and hand the case over to certain other men. He had deliberately let Cui Wentai believe that the people coming for the gold bars were of great importance.
He knew that Cui Wentai was the traitor within.
The afternoon before, coming away from Chen Qianyuan's and sitting on the bus, a single movement had flashed suddenly into his mind—a movement Old Fang had made.

On the day Old Fang died, he had charged out of the barbershop pistol in hand, fired a shot toward the mouth of the lane, and then run for the far end; but just as he was about to turn into the cross-lane, he had suddenly whirled and come running back toward the barbershop. Chen Qianli called up Old Fang's strange behavior and strained to remember the look on his face: Old Fang had not been looking at the enemy at the lane's mouth at all; his face had been turned toward the barbershop door, as though gazing at the men behind it.

It was as if he had remembered something, and wanted with all his heart to tell them—and in that very instant the bullet struck him. He must have known he could never make it back to the barbershop door; perhaps he had thought of shouting out what he had to say, but he could only duck behind the house at the corner of the cross-lane.

Chen Qianli changed to a tram and went straight to the lane of the barbershop. He walked up and down the lane as though searching for a house number, examining with care every spot Old Fang had reached after bursting from the shop, examining the ground and the corners of the walls—until, at one corner of the cross-lane, he found a single character. The place where it was written happened to be shielded by a drainpipe, so that the character was neither easy to see nor easily washed away by the rain.

The character had very likely been written by Old Fang in blood—his own blood. It was an unfinished 山, the word for “mountain.” At once Chen Qianli understood: Old Fang was hinting to him at the traitor's name. He did not know on what Old Fang had based the judgment; he guessed that perhaps Old Fang had suddenly recalled that of this secret meeting place, the barbershop, Cui Wentai was the only one who knew. It was very possible. Old Fang had looked on Cui Wentai as one of his own family.

Right up to the drawing of the operation plan, Chen Qianli had still had no hard proof that Cui Wentai was the traitor, the informer who had brought such ruin upon the organization. But on New Year's Eve Cui Wentai had let slip more that was suspect, and by morning, when Old Yi told Lin Shi that Cui Wentai had stolen into the consulting room in the dead of night, the truth was in fact wholly plain. Only the enemy did not yet know that he had guessed Cui Wentai to be the traitor. And it was precisely this that his plan meant to turn to account.

He had made the café his fall-back point, never thinking the enemy would be in that same lane. Any operation demanded a survey of the ground—paperwork alone could not be trusted—but he had had no time. In effect he had exposed Yi Junnian's position; Old Yi had been released from the detention house only a few days before, and the plainclothesmen of the detective squad might well recognize him. He ought to have found a more sheltered place.

No one had thought Cui Wentai would make off with the suitcase, and watching that scene Chen Qianli had felt, all at once, that there was something comic in it. He saw Cui Wentai's car turn back onto Tianjin Road, saw two men come running out of the lane to meet it, saw the car suddenly gun its engine and tear past the lane, saw the two men left standing in the road, unable for the longest time to make sense of it. That bolt of Cui Wentai's had turned a carefully plotted game of chess into a farce.

Had he himself foreseen this turn? Certainly not—yet he had indeed had Lin Shi tell everyone that there were five gold bars in the bank. It had been a kind of instinct, perhaps; it ran somewhat counter to the principles of underground work, but he had a dim sense that if you let certain men know they were holding a good many bars of gold, they would go about things all topsy-turvy, out of their ordinary character.

Standing on the roof of the bank, Chen Qianli had been anxious throughout. He did not know whether the enemy might not suddenly run mad and order everyone seized. Only when he caught sight of Ye Qinian did he feel he could breathe again. Even at that distance he could tell the man at a glance; he had no need even to take out the little telescope in the pocket of his fur gown. Ye Qinian was sitting in his car; by then Cui Wentai had long since fled, and Lin Shi and the others had withdrawn from the café. For some reason Chen Qianli had a feeling that made him want to stand on the roof and watch a while longer.

He watched Ye Qinian's car nose slowly out of the lane and halt at the intersection; someone came up to speak to him; he wound down the window, said a few words, then pushed the door open and got out, stood by the car looking left and right along the road, stared at the bank a while, and slowly raised his head, as though inspecting the bank building floor by floor. Only then was Chen Qianli certain that the enemy would probably not at once surround the comrades' lodgings and carry out a mass arrest. One look at Ye Qinian and he had known it in his heart: this spymaster never ran mad—not even when he had lost his own daughter.
They were waiting for him in a house near Gujiazhai Park, the key to which Wei Dafu had got from a rent-collecting agency.

Yi Junnian told Chen Qianli, “Once we were through the iron gate into the French Concession we got out, changed to a rickshaw, and came here.” Then he asked, “What kept you so long? We were worried you couldn't get clear.”
“I had to go to the secondhand-clothes shop and give back that costume,” Chen Qianli said with a laugh.
“Did Cui Wentai deliver the gold?” Yi Junnian asked.
“Cui Wentai never showed up at the appointed rendezvous. He ran off with the suitcase.” Chen Qianli told them the whole course of events, his face as calm as ever.
“So—there was no gold in the case?” Yi Junnian said, the light breaking on him.

So Ling Wen had not told Yi Junnian about switching the suitcases, Chen Qianli thought; perhaps she had not yet had the chance—or perhaps Ling Wen was truly a comrade who kept the discipline of underground work to the letter.
“I see it now—there was never any gold at all. You laid a trap to make Cui Wentai give himself away,” Yi Junnian said.

And give himself away he had. Chen Qianli told them that, by his reckoning, Cui Wentai had betrayed the revolution long ago. The meeting at the market, and the barbershop of Old Fang's son—both, surely, he had reported in secret to the enemy. “We've long suspected there was a traitor among us, and the traitor is most likely him.” And having said it, Chen Qianli thought: in truth, Old Fang had named him before he died.

Chen Qianli had come through a harsh training, in which he had been required again and again to pare away every unnecessary movement; yet Old Fang, at that instant between life and death, had suddenly made one baffling, superfluous movement. Why had Old Fang whirled and run back? Only when that question entered Chen Qianli's mind did he know what he himself had to do.
“I didn't tell you all beforehand,” Chen Qianli said with a smile, “because I was afraid that if you knew in advance, you wouldn't play your parts so convincingly.”

Of all the group who had attended the secret meeting that day, only Li Han had never come into the enemy's view. He had not been arrested, and after leaving the market he had made contact with no one. The Maochang coal yard lay on the edge of the Zhaojiabang, the creek that divided the Concession from the Chinese city; order on the two banks fell respectively to the Concession police and to the Nationalist public-security bureau. Around the yard stretched broad waste ground, and the people who lived there were in the main refugees who had fled to Shanghai, so the police paid the place little heed. Chen Qianli meant to have Lin Shi hide in the yard for the time being. Li Han said there would be no trouble at all: one word from him and the brothers in the yard would all lend a hand.

Ling Wen and the others had ridden in a car from the Nanshi police station, driven by an intelligence man Yi Junnian had cultivated inside the Nationalist public-security bureau. Though Yi Junnian assured them all the man was utterly to be trusted, he was not a member of the temporary action group, and so they had chosen to get out near Gujiazhai Park, and only after the car had driven off had Wei Dafu brought them here.

Toward four o'clock Wei Dafu went out to the street and called two rickshaws, and they set off. Lin Shi and Ling Wen each took a rickshaw and had the pullers take them to the little wooden bridge over the Zhaojiabang; the others went by separate ways. Chen Qianli and Yi Junnian went together, the one carrying a few slabs of soy-braised meat, the other a couple of bottles of wine, for all the world as though they meant to add a dish or two to some family's holiday table.
“There's something I don't quite follow,” Yi Junnian said as they turned from Rue Père Robert into Xujiahui Road. “Once Cui Wentai had the suitcase, why didn't they make their arrests at once?”
“It really isn't the detective squad's usual way. They were in no hurry to grab men and claim the credit. These enemies seem to have patience.”
Yi Junnian laughed. “You've only just come to Shanghai, and here you are talking as if you'd had years of dealings with the detective squad.”
A little abashed, Chen Qianli laughed too. “Then who, in your view, is our adversary this time?”
“These last two days I've been asking around about this You Tianxiao. Some say he's really an agent of the Special Operations Headquarters.”

“They don't want to simply seize a few Communists—they mean to play a long line and hook a big fish. By their methods, it really is more like that spearhead of the ‘bandit-suppression’ drive.” Yi Junnian was thoughtful. “They say this Special Operations Headquarters has several experts who do nothing but investigate the underground Party. They've gone to great lengths to study our working methods; when they crack an underground organization, they're in no hurry to kill. They'll learn every detail of a case, work it up into a training manual, and use it to train their agents. These past two years the underground Party has found Shanghai harder and harder going—Old Fang said a fair number of the Central leaders have already withdrawn to the Soviet areas.”

By dusk the sky had darkened in a moment, and all at once snowflakes came drifting down. They quickened their steps, crossed the bridge, and before them lay a great stretch of waste ground, with a scattering of shacks thrown up along the creek. The coal yard was easy to find: the coal was heaped in mounds like so many little hills, ringed about by a fence roughly cobbled together from wire and planks.

A little path ran through the waste ground along the creek, laid with coal cinders, weeds growing thick on either side; withered now in winter, they still stood knee-high. The snow fell faster and faster, and before long a layer of it lay over the black coal heaps, glinting in the twilight. At the coming of strangers the yard's watchdogs began to bark, and Li Han came running toward the sound; the other comrades had long since arrived.

A few single-story rooms stood hemmed in among the coal heaps, quite invisible from without: the yard's watch-room and tool sheds. Five or six of them ran together in a row. In ordinary times the workers came and went here, but now they had all gone home for the New Year, and with nothing doing no one would come this way. These few, though, in their dress and bearing, looked nothing like the sort who usually went into a coal yard, and to be seen would easily rouse suspicion; so Li Han, taking special care, had let the dogs out of their kennels early. Should any stranger blunder in, the dogs would set up a barking before he could come near.

They sat in the innermost room, a kettle steaming on the stove, the window filmed with frost. A single bulb burned in the room. The sky grew darker, and all around lay open waste ground: a house lit up too brightly could have been seen from the far bank of the Zhaojiabang.

The tabletop had perhaps once been a door-plank—thick, its surface unplaned and pitted with hollows; the legs, though, were sturdy enough, a frame welded up from iron plate and bar, with the door-plank laid across it.
On the table were wine, soy-braised meat, steamed buns, and a great heap of peanuts Li Han had brought.

“As things now stand across the country, our Party is holding to the road of revolution under conditions of extraordinary difficulty.” Lin Shi put a peanut into his mouth and spoke slowly. “After the counter-revolutionary governments of Ninghan and Ningyue merged one upon the other, Nanjing gained, on the surface, the semblance of a unified nation; Chiang Kai-shek declared the National Government entered upon its period of ‘political tutelage,’ built up the army, the police, the gendarmerie and the secret service with all his might, and bent his main energies upon a frenzied ‘suppression of the Communists.’ Our Party has met him point for point: as far back as the August 7th Conference we put it that the gun must be answered with the gun, that the broad masses of peasants in China's heartland must be roused to resist, and that an agrarian revolution must be set in motion.”
He announced to them all that the secret operation was now formally begun. This meeting, which should have been finished a fortnight before, had been put off all this while by unforeseen events—

“Time truly presses,” Lin Shi said at the last, “and drag it out too long, and the plan becomes hard to keep secret. The enemy is probing and wrecking the underground Party by every means they can contrive, and cases like Cui Wentai's have not been few of late. Comrade Qianli and I are of one mind: the enemy may already have guessed that the Party Central Committee is about to make some great move. Their letting us out of the detention house this time was no act of stupidity—far more likely it was a scheme.”

“Cui Wentai—you've only to look at that face to know he's no good. Cheekbones you can see from behind, the bone of a rebel in his skull.” Wei Dafu jabbed a finger at his own jaw, speaking with venom. “Grown square, this part of him. Set that face of his at the edge of a table, and you could tip a bowl over and the soup wouldn't reach the floor. Old Fang should never have trusted him so.”
“And our group—what do we do next?” Yi Junnian took out his cigarette case and lit one.

Lin Shi glanced at Liang Shichao, seated by the window, who every so often wiped the frost from the glass with a finger and looked out. Whenever Liang Shichao thought of how he had been taken in by Cui Wentai, it sat ill with him.

Lin Shi did not tell them that the Central Committee had in fact reconstituted its Liaison Bureau for this very purpose. Nor did he tell anyone but Chen Qianli that the true objective of the “A Thousand Li of Rivers and Mountains” plan was to carry out a great strategic transfer of the Central organs. Beyond what had to be conveyed, all the rest must be kept secret; that was the principle. His own code name was “Laokai,” the King—the thirteenth card in the deck.
